findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, so the scroll-stopping line is buried in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of BASH FUNCTIONS FIELD GUIDE. Your Bash function returned a string and the caller got nothing — because `return` only speaks in numbers 0–255..."
findings.fix: Lead with the pain: "Your Bash function returned a string and the caller got nothing — `return` only speaks in numbers 0–255." Move "Part 2 of BASH FUNCTIONS FIELD GUIDE" to the end of the caption, just before the hashtags.

findings.summary: The bullet claims the `EXIT` trap covers `return`, but a bash EXIT trap fires only when the shell itself exits — never when a function returns — which is exactly the wrong lesson in a guide about functions.
findings.evidence: "`EXIT` covers return, error, `set -e` and Ctrl-C exits" — in bash, `trap` is shell-global (a trap set inside a function stays in effect after the function returns), and the EXIT trap runs on shell exit, not on `return` from a function. `f(){ trap 'echo CLEANUP' EXIT; return 0; }; f; echo after` prints `after` first and `CLEANUP` only when the script ends.
findings.fix: Drop `return` from the list and say what actually happens: "`EXIT` covers normal end, `exit`, `set -e` aborts and Ctrl-C — but *not* a function `return`: traps are shell-global, so a trap set inside a function fires at script exit and overwrites any earlier `EXIT` trap." If per-call cleanup inside a function is wanted, show the `( ... )` subshell-plus-trap form instead.

findings.summary: Section 4 is titled "Why the Gap Leaks" but shows only the happy-path sequence, never demonstrating a gap or a leak.
findings.evidence: Heading "4. Why the Gap Leaks" followed by a flow diagram of `["mktemp -d","trap ... EXIT","real work","exit anywhere","dir removed"]` — the correct order, with nothing between mktemp and trap and no leak; the only mention of failure is the prose bullet "Any command before the trap can abort and leak".
findings.fix: Replace or precede the diagram with the failing case a learner can compare against, e.g. a two-line code block `tmp=$(mktemp -d)` / `validate "$1" || exit 1   # aborts here — trap never set, dir leaks` / `trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT`, and define "the gap" in the section's first line rather than only in the closing takeaway.

findings.summary: The page claims an EXIT trap fires on `return`, which in a handbook about functions reads as "fires when a function returns" — it does not.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "`EXIT` covers return, error, `set -e` and Ctrl-C exits", on a page that has already told the learner "A function call sets it from its `return` or last command".
findings.fix: Change the bullet to "`EXIT` fires only when the shell itself exits — normal end, `exit N`, `set -e` abort, or Ctrl-C — not when a function `return`s (that needs a `RETURN` trap with `set -T`)."

findings.summary: The table states `f | g` leaves g's status in `$?` as an unconditional rule, which is false under `set -o pipefail` — an option the same page implicitly assumes elsewhere by discussing `set -e`.
findings.evidence: Table row "`f | g` | g's status", while a later bullet says "`EXIT` covers ... `set -e`". With `set -o pipefail`, `false | true` yields `$?` = 1 (rightmost non-zero), not g's 0.
findings.fix: Qualify the row: "`f | g` → g's status (rightmost non-zero under `set -o pipefail`)", or add a one-line footnote under the table naming `pipefail` and `PIPESTATUS`.

findings.summary: `$!` and `wait` are introduced as the background-job alternative with no definition or example anywhere on the page.
findings.evidence: Bullet: "Background jobs use `$!` and `wait`, not `$?`" — `$!` appears once and is never expanded; the rest of the page is foreground-only.
findings.fix: Either cut the bullet from this page or give it the one line it needs: "`cmd & pid=$!; wait "$pid"` — `$!` is the background PID, and `wait` then puts that job's status in `$?`."

findings.summary: The sidebox prescribes a different cleanup command than the code block taught two sections earlier, without saying which one the learner should write.
findings.evidence: Code block teaches `trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT`; the later sidebox says "guard with `[[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -rf -- \"$tmp\"`".
findings.fix: Make the two agree — either promote the guarded form into the taught code block (`trap '[[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -rf -- "$tmp"' EXIT`), or add a clause to the sidebox noting the guard is only needed when `$tmp` is not set by a checked `mktemp -d` as shown above.
